unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision cuts two hinges that the first draft kept. The first is the Church-paragraph opening, where the dynamic theory accepts the Church's Cross as 'the force that attracts.' The p12 Constantine passage now follows 'economize the gods' without that frame. The second is the comparison with hiring occult force instead of building machines, so 'cheap' in p14 has no comparison point.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'Economize the gods' and 'Trust of State Religions' still imply the economic reading, and the p12 satire stays intelligible.

evidence.quote: The Church points out this force in the Cross, and history needs only to follow it.
All it asks is to find and follow the force that attracts. The Church points out this force in the Cross
Good taste forbids saying that Constantine the Great speculated as audaciously as a modern stock-broker
no one could afford to buy or construct a costly and complicated machine when he could hire an occult force at trifling expense.
Fetish-power was cheap and satisfactory, down to a certain point. Outside of it, the Roman world was incredibly poor.

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Prefix p12 with 'All it asks is to find and follow the force that attracts. The Church points out this force in the Cross, and history needs only to follow it.' Then open p14 with the source's 'no one could afford … trifling expense' sentence.
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: required (the essential section on Rome's fall, Constantine's trust and slave and fetish)
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: The Constantine satire and the slave/fetish economics read as assertions. They should read as the dynamic theory applying its method of assigning values to attracting forces.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Rome argument loses its 'follow the Cross' step and its machine-versus-fetish rationale

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The first draft had already dropped 'to decide a final test of force between the divine powers.' The revision also cuts Eugene's raising of Hercules. 'Society on both sides' now watches a match in which only the Cross is named, so the contest of gods behind 'bet on the gods' disappears.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'Rival' and 'both sides' still signal two parties. The plan allows Theodosius/Eugene to be trimmed.

evidence.quote: and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match, to decide a final test of force between the divine powers.
and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match.
Theodosius marched against his rival Eugene with the Cross for physical champion; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match.

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore 'and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans;' (about 12 words), or cut the Theodosius sentence entirely.
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: optional tradeoff, but a trimmed version must not leave a dangling 'both sides'
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: The image collapses into a human rivalry. The joke that the pagan and Christian divine powers are being tested like fighters is lost.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Boxing-match left with only one champion

unresolved_should_improve.claim: Three linked statements were cut by the revision; the first draft kept all three. The first is that society felt the Cross had failed to protect its Church. The second is that the Civitas Dei became the new sum of attraction with the same mechanical weakness. The third is that the new forces dropped 'at the precise moment' of the Civitas Dei's triumph. The 'outcry' and 'Yet the attraction remained constant' lose their causes. The compass/gunpowder passage also loses its irony.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'Against the Cross' implies disappointment. 'Civitas Dei' still recurs in p15 and p20.

evidence.quote: felt still more deeply the disappointment in its new power, the Cross, which had failed to protect its Church.
The Civitas Dei, in its turn, became the sum of attraction for the Western world, though it also showed the same weakness in mechanics
The Civitas Dei, in its turn, became the sum of attraction for the Western world, though it also showed the same weakness in mechanics that had wrecked the Civitas Romae.
The outcry against the Cross became so loud among Christians that Bishop Augustine of Hippo was led to write a famous treatise
at the precise moment when the Cross on one side and the Crescent on the other, proclaimed the complete triumph of the Civitas Dei.
the sudden, unexplained appearance of at least two new natural forces of the highest educational value in mechanics.

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore the source's 'The Civitas Dei, in its turn … wrecked the Civitas Romae.' Then append to p17 the source's 'Literally, these two forces … triumph of the Civitas Dei.'
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: required (the essential sections on Augustine and on the compass and gunpowder)
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: The thread the argument later relies on is thinned. That thread is the Civitas Dei as the force that Luther and the Puritans try to restore and that the new forces later displace.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Civitas Dei chain broken: the Cross's failure, the new attraction, and the ironic timing of compass and gunpowder

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision deletes the whole instruments paragraph, including Bacon's 'by instruments and helps' and the self-restraint gloss in the source. 'The success of this method' now follows a sentence about Franklin and a few score conductors. It also cuts the clause saying the leaders 'obeyed without understanding.'
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: p22 closes its Baconian thread with 'the Baconian law held good,' which partly supplies the referent.

evidence.quote: for his true followers science always meant self-restraint, obedience, sensitiveness to impulse from without.
Bacon foretold it: "Neither the naked hand nor the understanding, left to itself, can effect much.
The success of this method staggers belief. Evidently a new variety of mind had appeared.
dragged on by an attractive power in advance, which even the leaders obeyed without understanding

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Change p23 to 'The success of Bacon's method staggers belief,' or restore the two-sentence 'Neither the naked hand …' quotation.
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: required (the essential section on Bacon and the conductors)
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: Readers must reach back to 'the Baconian law' to find the method. The point that even Newton, Franklin and Watt were drawn involuntarily is weakened.
unresolved_should_improve.title: 'This method' now lacks Bacon's method as antecedent

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision cuts the clause disclaiming the knowledge needed to date Europe's greatest momentum. 'Such progress as the world made' now stands as a flat assertion.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'Rather recklessly' in p17 still hedges the 3000 B.C.–A.D. 300 claim.

evidence.quote: Only a historian of very exceptional knowledge would venture to say at what date between 3000 B.C. and 1000 A.D., the momentum of Europe was greatest
Only a historian of very exceptional knowledge would venture to say at what date between 3000 B.C. and 1000 A.D., the momentum of Europe was greatest;
Such progress as the world made consisted in economies of energy rather than in its development; it was proved in mathematics;

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore the 'Only a historian of very exceptional knowledge …' clause (about 25 words).
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: the plan requires hedges to be kept
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: This removes one of the voice's core moves, claimed ignorance set against sweeping generalization, at the point where the theory's antiquity claim is most speculative.
unresolved_should_improve.title: Self-deprecating hedge on ancient momentum removed

unresolved_should_improve.claim: The revision cuts the sentence that Church and State, theology and philosophy have always preached the theory. It also cuts the 'Science has proved …' sentence, both of which the first draft kept. 'Thus far, religion, philosophy, and science seem to go hand in hand' now summarizes agreement that the paragraph no longer shows.
unresolved_should_improve.counterevidence: 'Called God or Nature' still implies that the religious and naturalist positions overlap.

evidence.quote: Church and State, theology and philosophy, have always preached it, differing only in the allotment of energy between nature and man.
Church and State, theology and philosophy, have always preached it, differing only in the allotment of energy between nature and man.
Any schoolboy knows enough to object at once that it is the oldest and most universal of all theories. Whether the attractive energy has been called God or Nature

unresolved_should_improve.minimal_repair: Restore the 19-word 'Church and State …' sentence after the schoolboy objection.
unresolved_should_improve.plan_relation: required (the essential section on religion, philosophy and science diverging only at the edge)
unresolved_should_improve.reader_effect: The schoolboy objection goes unanswered. The divergence 'only there,' at chaos versus unity, loses its contrast with the shared ground before it.
unresolved_should_improve.title: 'Oldest theory' admission loses its reason and its three-way convergence
